chapter_theme: Twelve venbas on shrines (Idaimarudur, Tiruvottriyur, Tiruvarur, Kanchi, Kalatti, Viruppaiyur, Tiruvaiyaru, Kutralam), each a single plea tied to the place: when will the night of eating and thirsting end, the dust of the devotees' feet is the medicine for the nine-mouthed wound, the pilgrims running from festival to festival seek fire while the lamp burns, how many mothers and names must there be, let no other womb take me, and say the Lord's name before Death, the blind eye and the townsfolk's fire arrive.
structure_note: The place names in the margin (இடைமருது, ஒற்றி, திருவாரூர், திருக்காஞ்சி, கச்சிக்காரோணம், திருக்காளத்தி, திருவிருப்பையூர், திருவையாறு, குற்றாலம்) are the shrines each venba names in its last foot, as the தலப்பாடல் form requires. 400 and 407 are the hunger verses, 402 and 405 the body verses, 406, 409 and 410 the rebirth verses (409 and 410 are a pair on the tired mother, the tired Brahma and the poet's tired feet), and 411 the close, which 412 to 430 in the next chapter continue at Kutralam.

400.reading: Chewing, swallowing, then seeking water to put out the thirst: when will the dawn come for me, my King, Marudha who burned the three cities of those who did not think on the good, now that I have come to your presence?
400.nuance: The round of eating and drinking stands for the whole of embodied life, and என்று விடியும், when will it dawn, makes that life a night. The verse asks the Lord of Idaimarudur for release from the body's needs, not for food.

401.reading: Black-throated, three-eyed, beautiful like the cosmic egg, a sugarcane standing by the sea at Ottri of rising fame, that is sweet so that the bodies of his servants melt.
401.nuance: The one verse of the chapter that asks nothing: a description of the Lord of Tiruvottriyur as sugarcane, the standard figure for sweetness, with the body's melting (உடல் உருக) as the devotee's response. அண்டத்தைப் போல அழகியது compares the Lord to the cosmic egg, as the whole.

402.reading: For the wound with nine mouths that drips with discharge and stinks, I have come to know the medicine: the dust at the feet of the great ones in the street of Tiruvottriyur of the god of gods who ate the poison.
402.nuance: The body is a single wound with nine openings, and the cure is not a drug but the dust of the devotees' feet, which the poet knows as a fact (அறிந்துகொண்டேன்). கடு அருந்தும் தேவாதிதேவன் is Siva who drank the halahala poison, so the Lord who took in poison presides over the cure.

403.reading: All the tanks are holy water, all the sand is white ash, all the groves are the Lord's attendant hosts: this on earth is Siva's world, say the true ascetics again and again, Tiruvottriyur.
403.nuance: A shrine praise in the ordinary manner, with the three things found at any place (water, sand, trees) renamed as the three things of Saiva worship (holy water, ash, the ganas). The authority is the true ascetics (மெய்த்தவத்தோர்), not the poet.

404.reading: While the Lord of Arur is right here, you wander from town to town saying 'it is the festival in that town'; see, you are mutes who never seek the sign within; while the lamp is burning, you go looking for fire.
404.nuance: ஆரூரர் இங்கிருக்க has a plain and a coded reading: the Lord of Tiruvarur is here in this shrine, so why run to other towns' festivals; or the Lord is here within the body (உளக்குறிப்பு, the inner sign, in line 3), so why go anywhere. The lamp and the fire make the second reading the stronger, since the lamp is what the seeker already carries. Both readings stand.

405.reading: For the womb-mouth that sits two fingers above the dung-mouth you let your eyes be troubled; you lie dead in Tiruvarur's chariot street, you, for a stream of running water.
405.nuance: The verse locates the object of lust by its distance from the anus and names it by what passes through it, in the manner of 359. நீரோடும் தாரைக்கா நீ, 'for a channel of running water', is the one phrase in doubt: the urine passage, or the stream of tears; the plain reading is the first. செத்துக் கிடக்கின்றாய், you lie dead, is the poet's verdict on the man alive in the festival street.

406.reading: How many towns, how many houses, how many mothers who bore me, how many names given to call me: 'enough, enough', I said, yet every day you will not relieve my weariness, Ekamba, Ekamba; is it your holy play?
406.nuance: The count is of births, each with its own town, house, mother and name; எத்தனை four times makes the number itself the complaint. திருவிளையாட்டு, the Lord's play, is the Saiva account of why the world is as it is; the poet turns it into a question whether his rebirths are a game.

407.reading: Teacher who gladly gives to every living thing from the elephant to the ant: hunger presses hard on me, sinner that I am, Lord; it grips and wrings my ruined belly, Karonar.
407.nuance: The appeal is from the universal feeder to the one belly left out, and the belly is called பாழ் வயிறு, waste, as if hunger itself were a fault of the body. Read beside 416, where the poet refuses to go to food, the verse is the cost of that refusal.

408.reading: You will not give up lying, you will not leave off flesh, you will not think of the Lord of Kalatti, you will not do what is right, you will not give up hot anger, you will not recite the five holy letters: mind, what greatness have you?
408.nuance: Six refusals, three of them the moral commonplaces (truth, no flesh, no anger, right conduct) and two Saiva (thinking of the Lord, the five letters). The verse treats these as one list; the Kural's ethics and the mantra are not ranked.

409.reading: My mother's body is worn out, my legs are worn out from the strong deed, and Brahma's hand too is worn out: Lord, Siva who dwells at Viruppaiyur, keep me from going yet again into some other mother's womb.
409.nuance: Three parties tire: the mother who bears, Brahma who writes the fate on the forehead, and the soul that walks the round. வல்வினையேன், I of hard deeds, gives the cause of the walking, so the plea admits the births are earned.

410.reading: So that the earth's heat may cool, the sky's smoke may clear, the rare mother may rest, the hand of Brahma who composes may rest and this servant's feet may rest, look on me, Lord, Lord of Tiruvaiyaru.
410.nuance: The pair of 409, with the same three tired parties, and two more that are hard: மண்ணும் தணல் ஆற, வானும் புகை ஆற, the earth cooling and the sky's smoke clearing, may be the pyre's heat and smoke, so that the poet asks for a death that is the last, or the elements wearied by remaking him. கண் பார், look on me, asks only for the Lord's glance.

411.reading: Before Death comes, before the eyes film over, before the milk you drink runs out at the corners of the mouth, before the kin fall on you and weep, before the townsfolk burn you: speak the name of the Lord of Kutralam.
411.nuance: Five முன்னே, before, running from the far (Death's approach) to the near (the mouth that can no longer hold milk) and then past death to the mourners and the pyre. The thing to do in time is the smallest possible act, saying a name.

links.note: The body as a vessel with nine openings that seep filth: the Naladiyar's fool praises the pot that leaks from nine holes because its dark skin dazzles him; Pattinathar calls it a nine-mouthed wound and names the cure. The Naladiyar's image serves to shame desire, Pattinathar's to ask for medicine.

Both set the hut or wound of nine gates against medicine: Arunagirinathar kept trying worthless medicines and yogas for his ashen body until his mind cried enough and turned to the feet; Pattinathar says the one medicine for the stinking nine-mouthed wound is the dust of the devotees' feet. Both move the cure from the body to the feet.

Tirumular's people wander searching everywhere in the land for Nandi who is fragrant within the body and do not know the meaning that stands within it; Pattinathar's pilgrims run from festival to festival while the Lord of Arur is here and never seek the inner sign. Pattinathar adds the figure of seeking fire while the lamp burns.

The same method of breaking lust by naming the body's openings: 359 runs through the stinking mouth, eyes, body and yoni and asks how the mind clung; 405 fixes the womb-mouth two fingers above the dung-mouth and says the lover in the chariot street is already dead.

The Kural defines virtue as what proceeds without envy, craving, anger and harsh speech; Pattinathar's list of what the mind will not give up has lying, flesh and anger beside not thinking of the Lord and not reciting the five letters. The Kural's ethical list is kept and the Saiva items added to it as the same kind of thing.

Both ask for the end of rebirth after following the body to the fire: Arunagirinathar's townsfolk burn it to ash and he asks for grace not to seek this birth again; Pattinathar counts his mother, Brahma's hand and his own feet as worn out and asks not to enter another womb.

The Kural says do virtue without saying 'later', since at death it is the companion that does not perish; Pattinathar says speak the Lord's name before Death, the dimming eye, the mourners and the pyre. Both make the time before death the only time, and differ in what is to be done in it, virtue in the Kural and the name in Pattinathar.

The Naladiyar says the body lasts like water on a grass tip, so do good right now, for people will say 'he stood, he sat, he lay down, and with his kin wailing he was gone'; Pattinathar's five 'befores' end at the same wailing kin and the pyre. Both reason from the suddenness of the end to an act now.

source_issues: 402 line 4 has asterisks in the text (பெ*ரு*வாரடியிற்பொடி), an editor's mark of a doubtful reading; பெருவார் அடியிற் பொடி, the dust at the feet of the great, is assumed.
The place names printed beside the ids are editorial labels taken from each venba's last foot.
406 line 2 வேனென்றே / னித்த is broken by the line division: read வேண்டேன் என்றேன் நித்தம்.
